accepted_phrases: Arrow keys serve real navigation functions and software can remap functional layouts. The K12 exposes arrows through Fn combinations, while the K6 explicitly supplies dedicated arrows. One long-term HHKB owner reports that layered arrows became natural muscle memory, while another buyer rejects 60 percent specifically to retain arrows. Because this commuter prioritizes direct arrows and modifier shortcuts, the K6 fits the stated workflow unless a hands-on K12 trial changes that preference.

The K12 and MX Keys Mini runtime statements depend on backlight conditions, and the K6 body contains materially different up-to-10-hour, up-to-72-hour, and nine-normal-use-day statements. The Corne discussion shows large effects from display, LED, battery and configuration choices, but its custom-build anecdotes cannot predict any candidate. All three product runtimes remain conditional seller claims rather than observed commute endurance.

Bluetooth is a short-range low-power wire-replacement protocol used for keyboard communication, but neither that generic description nor any frozen product body measures product-specific end-to-end latency or perceptibility. Bluetooth 5.1 and Low Energy labels do not prove imperceptible lag. K12 and K6 explicitly provide wired keyboard input as a fallback, while the MX Keys Mini body's USB-C rechargeable wording is not evidence of wired input.

The frozen K12 is $99.99 with no reviews, a 60 percent 61-key layout, Fn-layer arrows, Bluetooth 5.1, wired Type-C input and a conditional 240-hour claim. The K6 is $83.99 with no reviews, a 65 percent 68-key layout, dedicated arrows, Bluetooth 5.1, wired Type-C input, 317 by 107 by 37 millimetre dimensions, 2.25-pound weight and internally different conditional runtime statements. The MX Keys Mini is $99.99 with 52/100 from 12 reviews, Bluetooth Low Energy, a thinner and lighter profile and a conditional 10-day or five-month claim, but no stated wired keyboard input. None supplies measured Bluetooth typing latency.
